title: Infantile Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis
subject: Surgery
summary: A congenital thickening of the pyloric muscle blocks gastric emptying, causing projectile vomiting and dehydration in the first weeks of life. Diagnosis is clinical plus ultrasound, and treatment is surgical pyloromyotomy.

sections.p: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) is a congenital thickening of the pyloric circular muscle that progressively obstructs gastric outlet. Classic presentation is projectile, non‑bilious vomiting in a 2–8‑week‑old infant. Diagnosis is confirmed by abdominal ultrasound showing a pyloric channel length >14 mm and muscle thickness >4 mm.

t.b: Is the pyloric channel thickened? A length >14 mm and thickness >4 mm confirm IHPS.

t.a: Physical exam – palpation of the olive
t.b: Can the olive be felt in the epigastrium? A palpable olive suggests pyloric hypertrophy.

sections.p: Severity is mainly clinical: dehydration, weight loss, and electrolyte imbalance. Ultrasound findings guide surgical timing but do not alter staging.
IHPS is a sporadic developmental anomaly; the exact trigger is unknown. In low‑resource settings, consider maternal malnutrition, low birth weight, and possible herbal supplements as risk modifiers.
The infant vomits forcefully after feeds, often with a visible projectile. The baby is dehydrated, lethargic, and may have a palpable olive in the right upper quadrant. Bilious vomiting is absent.
Investigations confirm the diagnosis and assess for complications.

t.b: Is the chloride low (<30 mmol/L) indicating renal loss? A low urine chloride supports a non‑renal cause of alkalosis.
Rule out other causes of vomiting? A normal X‑ray with no obstruction supports IHPS.

sections.p: Urgent red flags include severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, or failure to thrive. Complications may be perforation, aspiration, or postoperative ileus.
Management is staged: pre‑operative stabilization, definitive surgery, and postoperative care.

t.b: Start small, frequent feeds to assess tolerance; monitor for residual vomiting.

sections.p: Follow‑up focuses on weight gain and hydration. Prevention is not established; focus on early recognition.
Other causes of projectile vomiting include gastroenteritis, pyloric ulcer, and intestinal obstruction.
Metabolic alkalosis can be seen in other conditions like vomiting from gastroenteritis; chloride levels may be normal if dehydration is severe.
Seek urgent care if the infant shows signs of severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, or failure to thrive.

faq.q: Why is the vomiting non‑bilious in IHPS?
faq.a: Because the obstruction is proximal to the bile duct entry, so bile does not mix with gastric contents.
Recurrence is rare if the pyloromyotomy is complete; incomplete cuts can lead to residual obstruction.

faq.q: What is the typical age of presentation?
faq.a: Most infants present between 2 and 8 weeks of age, with a peak around 4 weeks.

exam: What is the most specific ultrasound finding for IHPS? — Pyloric channel length >14 mm and muscle thickness >4 mm.
A 3‑week‑old infant presents with projectile vomiting. Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely? — Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
You suspect IHPS but the infant is severely dehydrated. What is the first step? — Rapid IV fluid resuscitation and correction of electrolytes.
Why is a pyloromyotomy preferred over resection? — It preserves gastric function and has lower morbidity.
An infant with projectile vomiting has a palpable olive. What is the next best investigation? — Abdominal ultrasound.
A postoperative infant continues to vomit. What complication should you consider? — Post‑operative ileus or incomplete pyloromyotomy.
